```{python}
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyBboxPatch


shade = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("shade", ["#bfe0b0", "#ffffff", "#f5b8cb"])


def scoreboard(table, rules=None, by="column", decimals=3):
    """A results table in Great Tables: green is better, pink is worse, the best in bold.

    rules maps a metric to "lower", "higher" or a target value (default: every column "lower").
    by="column" compares the rows of each column; by="row" shades each metric on one scale
    and bolds the best of each row.
    """
    df = table.to_frame() if isinstance(table, pd.Series) else table.copy()
    df.index = [str(i) for i in df.index]
    nested = isinstance(df.columns, pd.MultiIndex)
    groups = list(dict.fromkeys(df.columns.get_level_values(0))) if nested else []
    df.columns = ["|".join(map(str, c)) if nested else str(c) for c in df.columns]
    metric = {c: c.split("|")[-1] for c in df.columns}
    rules = rules or {m: "lower" for m in metric.values()}

    gt = (GT(df.reset_index(names="row"), rowname_col="row")
          .fmt_number(columns=list(df.select_dtypes("number").columns), decimals=decimals)
          .sub_missing(missing_text="")
          .cols_label(cases=metric)
          .tab_options(table_font_size="0.75em", data_row_padding="4px"))
    for g in groups:
        gt = gt.tab_spanner(label=g, columns=[c for c in df.columns if c.startswith(f"{g}|")])

    for m, rule in rules.items():
        cols = [c for c in df.columns if metric[c] == m]
        values = df[cols].astype(float)
        bad = values if rule == "lower" else -values if rule == "higher" else (values - rule).abs()
        blocks = [bad[[c]] for c in cols] if by == "column" else [bad]
        for block in blocks:
            lo, hi = np.nanmin(block.values), np.nanmax(block.values)
            for c in block.columns:
                for i, b in enumerate(block[c]):
                    if np.isnan(b):
                        continue
                    fill = to_hex(shade((b - lo) / (hi - lo) if hi > lo else 0.0))
                    best = b == (block[c].min() if by == "column" else bad.iloc[i].min())
                    look = [gt_style.fill(color=fill)] + ([gt_style.text(weight="bold")] if best else [])
                    gt = gt.tab_style(style=look, locations=loc.body(columns=c, rows=[i]))
    return gt


def draw_net(ax, layers, labels, colours, title=""):
    """A small fully connected network: one column of circles per layer, every edge drawn."""
    xs = np.linspace(0, 1, len(layers))
    nodes = []
    for x, n, names, colour in zip(xs, layers, labels, colours):
        ys = np.linspace(0.5 + 0.13 * (n - 1), 0.5 - 0.13 * (n - 1), n)
        nodes.append([(x, y) for y in ys])
        for (cx, cy), name in zip(nodes[-1], names):
            ax.add_patch(Circle((cx, cy), 0.045, facecolor="white", edgecolor=colour, linewidth=2, zorder=3))
            ax.text(cx, cy, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, zorder=4)
    for left, right in zip(nodes[:-1], nodes[1:]):
        for a in left:
            for b in right:
                ax.plot([a[0] + 0.045, b[0] - 0.045], [a[1], b[1]], color="grey", linewidth=0.8, zorder=1)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 1.1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title)
```

# Where this fits

## Eight weeks of local models {.smaller}

Every model so far has been **local**: fitted to one series, with its own parameters, knowing nothing
about any other series.

| Week | Model | Learns from |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 3 | benchmarks | one series, one rule |
| 2 | decomposition | one series |
| 4 | ETS | one series |
| 5 | regression | one series and its predictors |
| 6, 7 | ARIMA, dynamic regression | one series and its predictors |
| 8 | MSTL, harmonic regression, Prophet, combinations | one series |

Your Track B series has between 56 and 264 observations. Every parameter of your Lab 7 ARIMA was
estimated from those, and nothing else.

## Three steps away from "one series" {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**1. Non-linear, still local**

*Neural network autoregression.* The same lags as an AR model, but the forecast is a non-linear
function of them.

One series. Hundreds of observations.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**2. Global**

*LightGBM on lags, N-HiTS, LSTM.* One model trained on **many series at once**; each series borrows
the patterns of the others.

One dataset. Thousands of series.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**3. Pretrained**

*Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai.* One model trained on **millions of series** from many domains, then
applied to yours with **no training at all**.

Your series. Zero fitted parameters.
:::
::::

The question for each step is the same one we have asked for eight weeks: **does it beat the benchmark
on a holdout it never saw?** — and, new this week, *how do we know it never saw it?*

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading

[FPP3 §12.4 neural network models](https://otexts.com/fpp3/nnetar.html) ·
[Ansari et al. (2024), *Chronos*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07815) ·
[Ansari et al. (2025), *Chronos-2*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15821) ·
M. Peixeiro, *Time Series Forecasting Using Foundation Models* (Manning, 2025)
:::

# Neural network autoregression

## An AR model is a network with no hidden layer {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
\hat y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \phi_3 y_{t-3}
$$

| Time series | Neural networks |
|---|---|
| lags $y_{t-i}$ | inputs |
| coefficients $\phi_i$ | weights |
| intercept $c$ | bias |
| least squares | training on squared loss |

A linear regression on lags **is** a neural network — one with no hidden layer and no activation.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
#| label: ar-as-net
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
draw_net(ax, [3, 1], [["$y_{t-1}$", "$y_{t-2}$", "$y_{t-3}$"], [r"$\hat y_t$"]],
         [blue, red_pink], "AR(3): inputs straight to the output")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

## Add a hidden layer {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Each hidden neuron takes its own weighted sum of the lags and squeezes it through a non-linear
**activation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_j &= b_j + \sum_{i=1}^{p} w_{ij}\, y_{t-i}\\[2pt]
h_j &= s(z_j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z_j}}\\[2pt]
\hat y_t &= a + \sum_{j=1}^{k} v_j\, h_j
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| label: nnar-net
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
draw_net(ax, [3, 4, 1], [["$y_{t-1}$", "$y_{t-2}$", "$y_{t-3}$"], ["$h_1$", "$h_2$", "$h_3$", "$h_4$"],
                         [r"$\hat y_t$"]],
         [blue, turquoise, red_pink], "NNAR(3, 4): one hidden layer")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

$k$ hidden neurons, each a different "view" of the lags. The sigmoid is what makes the model
non-linear — without it the network collapses back to an AR model. Weights start at random values and
are fitted by gradient descent on the squared error.

## NNAR$(p, P, k)_m$ {.smaller}

The model in FPP3 §12.4 — `nnetar()` in R — is exactly this network, with conventions that make it a
forecasting method:

- **Inputs:** $p$ ordinary lags $y_{t-1}, \dots, y_{t-p}$ and $P$ seasonal lags $y_{t-m}, \dots, y_{t-Pm}$.
- **Hidden layer:** one, with $k$ neurons. Default $k = (p + P + 1)/2$, rounded.
- **Defaults for $p$:** the order of the best AR model on the seasonally adjusted series; $P = 1$.
- **Twenty networks**, each from different random starting weights, and their forecasts **averaged**
  — a combination (Week 8) used to tame the randomness of training.
- Inputs are **scaled** first; a network trains badly on raw values in the thousands.

NNAR$(p, 0, k)$ is the non-seasonal version — the one we fit next.

## Sunspots: a non-linear series {.smaller}

The yearly mean number of sunspots, 1700–2008 — Yule fitted the first autoregressive model to this
series in 1927.

```{python}
#| label: sunspots
#| fig-align: center
spots = sm.datasets.sunspots.load_pandas().data
spots["year"] = spots["YEAR"].astype(int)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4), width_ratios=[2.2, 1])
axes[0].plot(spots["year"], spots["SUNACTIVITY"], color=slate, linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Yearly sunspot number")
cycle = spots.query("1933 <= year <= 1944")
axes[1].plot(cycle["year"], cycle["SUNACTIVITY"], "o-", color=red_pink)
axes[1].set_title("One cycle: up in 4 years, down in 7")
plt.show()
```

The cycles are **asymmetric** — a fast rise, a slow decline — and peaks vary in height. A linear AR
model produces only symmetric cycles: up and down are the same equation.

## Fitting NNAR(9, 5) by hand {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
y_ss = np.sqrt(spots["SUNACTIVITY"].to_numpy())    # square root keeps the forecasts positive
H_SS = 30
train_ss, test_ss = y_ss[:-H_SS], y_ss[-H_SS:]
p, k = 9, 5
mu, sd = train_ss.mean(), train_ss.std()
z = (train_ss - mu) / sd                            # scale the inputs


def lag_matrix(z, p):
    X = np.column_stack([z[p - i - 1:len(z) - i - 1] for i in range(p)])   # y_{t-1}, ..., y_{t-p}
    return X, z[p:]


X, target = lag_matrix(z, p)
nets = [MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(k,), activation="logistic", alpha=1e-3,
                     max_iter=5000, random_state=seed).fit(X, target)
        for seed in range(20)]                                             # twenty networks
print(f"{len(target)} training rows, {p} inputs, {k} hidden neurons, "
      f"{p * k + k + k + 1} weights per network")
```

## Forecasting: one step at a time {.smaller}

A network predicts **one step ahead**. For $h > 1$ the forecast is fed back as if it were data — the
same recursion as ARIMA, but through a non-linear function:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
def nnar_forecast(nets, z, h, noise=None, rng=None):
    history, out = list(z[-p:]), []
    for _ in range(h):
        x = np.array(history[::-1][:p])[None, :]               # the latest p values, newest first
        value = np.mean([net.predict(x)[0] for net in nets])   # average of the twenty networks
        if noise is not None:
            value += rng.choice(noise)                         # a resampled training error
        out.append(value)
        history.append(value)
    return np.array(out)


point_ss = (nnar_forecast(nets, z, H_SS) * sd + mu) ** 2      # back to the sunspot scale
```

There is no formula for the forecast variance of a non-linear model. FPP's answer: **simulate**. Add a
resampled training error at every step, repeat many times, and read the interval off the paths.

## The simulated paths {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: nnar-paths
#| fig-align: center
residuals_ss = target - np.mean([net.predict(X) for net in nets], axis=0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
paths_ss = np.array([(nnar_forecast(nets, z, H_SS, residuals_ss, rng) * sd + mu) ** 2 for _ in range(300)])
lo80, hi80 = np.percentile(paths_ss, [10, 90], axis=0)
years_test = spots["year"].to_numpy()[-H_SS:]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.8))
ax.plot(spots["year"], spots["SUNACTIVITY"], color=slate, linewidth=1, label="sunspots")
for path in paths_ss[:12]:
    ax.plot(years_test, path, color=turquoise, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0.8)
ax.fill_between(years_test, lo80, hi80, color=red_pink, alpha=0.18, label="80% of 300 paths")
ax.plot(years_test, point_ss, color=red_pink, linewidth=2, label="NNAR(9, 5) forecast")
ax.set_xlim(1900, 2009)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("Thirty years ahead from 1978: twelve of the simulated paths, and the interval from all of them")
plt.show()
```

Three cycles ahead, the forecast keeps their **timing** and the fast-rise, slow-fall shape — not their
**height**: averaging damps every peak to about 100, and the two real peaks above 150 fall outside the
80% band. Single paths reach those heights; their average cannot.

## Scored on the thirty held-out years {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
arima_ss = AutoARIMA().fit(train_ss)
ets_ss = AutoETS().fit(train_ss)
truth = test_ss ** 2
candidates_ss = {
    "NNAR(9, 5)": point_ss,
    str(ARIMASummary(arima_ss.model_)): arima_ss.predict(H_SS)["mean"] ** 2,
    "AutoETS": ets_ss.predict(H_SS)["mean"] ** 2,
    "mean of the training years": np.full(H_SS, (train_ss ** 2).mean()),
}
scoreboard(pd.DataFrame({
    name: {"MAE": np.mean(np.abs(truth - f)),
           "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((truth - f) ** 2))}
    for name, f in candidates_ss.items()}).T, decimals=1)
```

- The network's error is about **a third lower** than the ARIMA's — both fitted on the same
  square-root scale, both forecasting 30 years.
- ETS, which has no cycles at all, does no better than the mean of the training years.
- This is the case NNAR was built for: a **long** series (270 training rows) with **genuinely
  non-linear** dynamics.

## What NNAR is, and is not {.smaller}

- **Is:** an autoregression that can bend. When the dynamics are genuinely non-linear — asymmetric
  cycles, thresholds, saturation — it can see what a linear model cannot.
- **Is not:** interpretable. 56 weights per network, twenty networks; there is no $\phi_1$ to read.
- **Is not:** stable without care. Different seeds give different networks; that is why it averages
  twenty.
- **Is not:** data-efficient. Sunspots give 300 years; your Track B series gives 56 to 264
  observations, and a network with 56 weights per 100 points is fitting noise.

[That last point is the real limit of a local network — and the reason the next two sections train on
many series at once.]{.hi}

# Global models

## Local and global {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Local** — one model per series

- $N$ series → $N$ sets of parameters.
- Each set is estimated from one series.
- ETS, ARIMA, NNAR, Prophet.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Global** — one model for all

- $N$ series → **one** set of parameters.
- Estimated from every window of every series.
- A seasonal shape seen in 500 series helps forecast the 501st.
:::
::::

A global model needs the series to be **comparable**, so each one is scaled by its own level first.
After that, it learns "what happens after a pattern like this", pooled over everything it has seen.

Evidence from the competitions: in **M4** (2018) the winner was a hybrid — exponential smoothing inside a
recurrent network trained across series — and the pure machine-learning entries did worse than the
statistical benchmarks. In **M5** (2020), on tens of thousands of Walmart series, the top of the
leaderboard was dominated by **LightGBM** trained globally.

## The data for this section: M3 Monthly {.smaller}

The 1428 monthly series of the **M3 competition** (Makridakis & Hibon, 2000) — micro, industry, macro,
finance, demographic — each with its last **18 months** held out, as in the competition.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
m3 = pd.read_csv("../data/m3_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
H_M3 = 18
test_m3 = m3.groupby("unique_id").tail(H_M3)
train_m3 = m3.drop(test_m3.index)
lengths = train_m3.groupby("unique_id").size()
print(f"{m3['unique_id'].nunique()} series; training length {lengths.min()} to {lengths.max()} months, "
      f"median {lengths.median():.0f}")
```

Every model in the rest of this lecture is scored on these same 1428 × 18 held-out months, by MASE with
$m = 12$ — the metric you have used since Week 3.

## The local baseline {.smaller}

Three local models, 1428 fits each — and the Week 8 combination of two of them:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
local = StatsForecast(models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12, alias="snaive"),
                              AutoETS(season_length=12, alias="ETS"),
                              AutoTheta(season_length=12, alias="Theta")],
                      freq="MS")
forecasts = test_m3.merge(local.forecast(df=train_m3, h=H_M3), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
forecasts["ETS + Theta"] = (forecasts["ETS"] + forecasts["Theta"]) / 2
```

The **Theta** method won M3 in 2000. It is simple exponential smoothing with drift — Week 4 — on a
seasonally adjusted series, and it remains one of the hardest benchmarks to beat on this data.

```{python}
#| include: false
scale_m3 = train_m3.groupby("unique_id")["y"].apply(lambda s: np.mean(np.abs(s.to_numpy()[12:] - s.to_numpy()[:-12])))


def m3_board(columns):
    err = forecasts.groupby("unique_id").apply(
        lambda g: pd.Series({c: np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g[c])) for c in columns}), include_groups=False)
    mase_m3 = err.div(scale_m3, axis=0)
    return pd.DataFrame({"mean MASE": mase_m3.mean(), "median MASE": mase_m3.median(),
                         "beats ETS on": mase_m3.lt(mase_m3["ETS"], axis=0).mean()})
```

## A global LightGBM on lags {.smaller}

The M5 recipe: a gradient-boosted tree model, **one** for all 1428 series, on lag features. Week 7's
dynamic regression with the lags as predictors — except that a tree finds the non-linearities itself.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from mlforecast import MLForecast
from mlforecast.target_transforms import Differences, LocalStandardScaler
import lightgbm as lgb

boosted = MLForecast(
    models={"LightGBM": lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=-1)},
    freq="MS",
    lags=[1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 24],                                   # the features
    date_features=["month"],
    target_transforms=[Differences([12]), LocalStandardScaler()],   # D = 1, then each series scaled
)
boosted.fit(train_m3)
forecasts = forecasts.merge(boosted.predict(H_M3), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
```

- `Differences([12])` is Week 7's seasonal difference; `LocalStandardScaler` puts every series on one
  scale, which is what makes **pooling** them possible.
- Forecasts are recursive, as for NNAR: each prediction becomes a lag for the next.

One reasonable configuration, the kind you would try first — **not tuned**. Tuning a global model is a
project of its own; the scored table below is what you get on the first attempt.

# Neural networks for sequences

## Recurrent networks: a memory that is carried forward {.smaller}

NNAR sees a **fixed window** of $p$ lags. A recurrent network (RNN) reads the series one value at a time
and carries a **hidden state** $h_t$ — a vector summary of everything so far:

$$
h_t = \tanh\left(W h_{t-1} + U y_t + b\right), \qquad \hat y_{t+1} = V h_t + c
$$

```{python}
#| label: rnn-unrolled
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.1))
for i, t in enumerate(["t-2", "t-1", "t", "t+1"]):
    x = i * 2.2
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, 0.8), 1.2, 0.8, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05", facecolor="white",
                                edgecolor=turquoise, linewidth=2))
    ax.text(x + 0.6, 1.2, f"$h_{{{t}}}$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x + 0.6, 0.78), xytext=(x + 0.6, 0.1), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=blue))
    ax.text(x + 0.6, -0.05, f"$y_{{{t}}}$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=13)
    if i < 3:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + 2.18, 1.2), xytext=(x + 1.27, 1.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=red_pink, lw=2))
        ax.text(x + 1.72, 1.32, "$W$", color=red_pink, fontsize=12, ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 8.2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.8)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("The same weights $W, U$ at every step: the network unrolled through time")
plt.show()
```

No fixed window, and the **same** weights at every step — as ARIMA's recursion is to a regression on
fixed lags.

## Why plain RNNs forget, and what LSTM does about it {.smaller}

Training an RNN multiplies by $W$ once per step back in time. Over many steps the gradient shrinks to
nothing (**vanishing**) or blows up (**exploding**) — so a plain RNN cannot learn that December depends
on last December.

The **LSTM** (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a second state $c_t$, the **cell**, changed only by
gated, mostly additive updates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_t &= \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1}, y_t] + b_f) & &\text{forget: how much of } c_{t-1} \text{ to keep}\\
i_t &= \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1}, y_t] + b_i) & &\text{input: how much new to write}\\
c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tanh(W_c[h_{t-1}, y_t] + b_c) & &\text{the cell: additive update}\\
o_t &= \sigma(W_o[h_{t-1}, y_t] + b_o), \quad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) & &\text{output}
\end{aligned}
$$

Each gate is a sigmoid between 0 and 1. With $f_t \approx 1$ the cell passes information — and gradient —
through many steps unchanged. It is the same idea as ETS's level equation: **keep most of the old state,
add a little of the new**.

## The architectures you will meet {.smaller}

| Model | Year | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **DeepAR** | 2020 | a global LSTM that outputs a **distribution**; intervals by sampling |
| **N-BEATS** | 2020 | no recurrence: stacked fully connected blocks, each passing on its residual |
| **N-HiTS** | 2023 | N-BEATS with blocks at several time resolutions; fast, long horizons |
| **TFT** | 2021 | attention plus gating, built for covariates |
| **PatchTST** | 2023 | a transformer reading the series in **patches** of values, like words |

: {tbl-colwidths="[16,8,76]"}

All of them in Python: [`neuralforecast`](https://nixtlaverse.nixtla.io/neuralforecast/) — the same
`fit` / `predict` / `cross_validation` interface as `statsforecast`.

## N-HiTS and an LSTM on M3 {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.models import LSTM, NHITS

quiet = dict(enable_progress_bar=False, logger=False, enable_model_summary=False)
neural = NeuralForecast(
    models=[NHITS(h=H_M3, input_size=24, scaler_type="robust", max_steps=600, random_seed=1, **quiet),
            LSTM(h=H_M3, input_size=24, scaler_type="robust", max_steps=600, random_seed=1, **quiet)],
    freq="MS")
neural.fit(train_m3)                        # one network of each kind, trained on all 1428 series
forecasts = forecasts.merge(neural.predict(), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
```

- `input_size=24`: each training example is a window of 24 months and the 18 that follow, cut from
  every series — tens of thousands of windows.
- `scaler_type="robust"`: each window scaled by its own median and spread — the global model's
  equivalent of Week 7's log.

Both train in about a minute on a laptop CPU. Again one configuration, not tuned, with one fixed seed —
report the seed, because a network trained from another starting point is a different model.

## The global models, scored {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
scoreboard(m3_board(["snaive", "ETS", "Theta", "ETS + Theta",
                     "LightGBM", "NHITS", "LSTM"]),
           rules={"mean MASE": "lower", "median MASE": "lower",
                  "beats ETS on": "higher"})
```

- **On M3 the global models do not beat the local ones.** N-HiTS is level with ETS; LightGBM and the
  LSTM are clearly worse, though both still beat seasonal naive.
- M3 is home ground for local models: **short** series (median 115 months) from **unrelated** domains —
  little that pooling can borrow. Global models win where series are many, long and alike: M5's
  products from one retailer.
- The best on this board is still Week 8's: the average of ETS and Theta.

# Foundation models

## Pretrain once, forecast anything {.smaller}

The step from global to **pretrained** is the step from "all the series in this dataset" to "all the
series we could find":

| | Trained on | At forecast time |
|---|---|---|
| Local (ETS, ARIMA) | your series | fit, then forecast |
| Global (LightGBM, N-HiTS) | your dataset | fit, then forecast |
| **Pretrained** (Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai) | **millions of other series** | **forecast only — zero-shot** |

The analogy is a large language model: trained once on a vast corpus, then asked about text it has
never seen. Here the "text" is your history, and the "answer" is its continuation.

Chronos (Amazon, 2024): 28 datasets, about **890,000** series and 84 billion observations, plus a
million synthetic ones. Your series is not one of them — or so we hope; this section ends on that word.

## How Chronos reads a time series {.smaller}

A language model needs **tokens** from a fixed vocabulary. Chronos makes them in two steps:

1. **Scale** each context by its mean absolute value: $\tilde y_t = y_t / s$, $\;s = \frac{1}{C}\sum |y_t|$.
2. **Quantise**: split $[-15, 15]$ into 4094 bins; each $\tilde y_t$ becomes the number of its bin.

```{python}
#| label: tokens
#| fig-align: center
air = pd.read_csv("../data/air_passengers.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
context = air["y"].to_numpy()[-48:]
scaled = context / np.mean(np.abs(context))
edges = np.linspace(0.4, 1.6, 13)                               # 12 coarse bins, for display only
tokens = np.digitize(scaled, edges)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3))
axes[0].plot(air["ds"].iloc[-48:], scaled, "o-", color=slate, markersize=3)
for e in edges:
    axes[0].axhline(e, color=turquoise, linewidth=0.5)
axes[0].set_title("Scaled air passengers, with the bin edges")
axes[1].step(range(48), tokens, where="mid", color=red_pink)
axes[1].set_title("The same series as a sequence of tokens (bin numbers)")
plt.show()
```

Then an ordinary **T5 language model** is trained to predict the next token — cross-entropy, as for
words. Forecasting is **sampling**: draw the next token, append, repeat; many sampled paths give the
quantiles. (The real vocabulary is 4096 tokens, not 12.)

## Chronos-Bolt and Chronos-2 {.smaller}

The original Chronos samples one token at a time — accurate, slow. The two successors you would use now:

- **Chronos-Bolt** (2024): reads the context in **patches** and outputs the quantiles of all $h$
  steps **directly**, with no sampling — up to 250 times faster. The small version, 48M parameters,
  forecasts a thousand series on a laptop CPU in seconds.
- **Chronos-2** (October 2025, 120M parameters): **group attention** lets several series in a group
  see each other — so it can use **covariates**, past-only or known in advance, which Chronos and
  Chronos-Bolt cannot.

Others you will see in papers and benchmarks: **TimesFM** (Google), **Moirai** (Salesforce), **TiRex**
(NX-AI), **Toto** (Datadog) — open weights, like Chronos — and **TimeGPT** (Nixtla), a commercial API: your
data leaves your machine.

## Zero-shot in four lines {.smaller}

The whole of "fitting" a foundation model:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from chronos import BaseChronosPipeline

bolt = BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-bolt-small", device_map="cpu")
context_m3 = [torch.tensor(g["y"].to_numpy(), dtype=torch.float32)
              for _, g in train_m3.groupby("unique_id", sort=True)]
quantiles, mean = bolt.predict_quantiles(context_m3, prediction_length=H_M3,
                                         quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
```

```{python}
#| include: false
order = sorted(train_m3["unique_id"].unique())
ds_sorted = test_m3.sort_values(["unique_id", "ds"])["ds"].to_numpy()


def as_frame(alias, values):
    return pd.DataFrame({"unique_id": np.repeat(order, H_M3), "ds": ds_sorted,
                         alias: np.concatenate([np.asarray(v).ravel()[:H_M3] for v in values])})


forecasts = forecasts.merge(as_frame("Chronos-Bolt", mean), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
bolt_lo = np.concatenate([np.asarray(q[:, 0]).ravel() for q in quantiles])
bolt_hi = np.concatenate([np.asarray(q[:, 2]).ravel() for q in quantiles])
```

No training step, no orders to choose, no seasonal period declared. The model was never told these
series are monthly — it reads the season off the context. Chronos-2 is the same call with
`"amazon/chronos-2"`.

```{python}
#| include: false
chronos2 = BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cpu")
_, mean2 = chronos2.predict_quantiles(context_m3, prediction_length=H_M3, quantile_levels=[0.5])
forecasts = forecasts.merge(as_frame("Chronos-2", mean2), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
```

## Everything on M3, scored {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
scoreboard(m3_board(["snaive", "ETS", "Theta", "ETS + Theta",
                     "LightGBM", "NHITS", "LSTM",
                     "Chronos-Bolt", "Chronos-2"]),
           rules={"mean MASE": "lower", "median MASE": "lower",
                  "beats ETS on": "higher"})
```

- **Chronos-2, never trained on these series, has the lowest error on the board** — about 6% below
  ETS, better than ETS on 58% of series, and ahead of the ETS + Theta average.
- **Chronos-Bolt** is level with ETS: an ETS-quality forecast for 1428 series in seconds.
- M3 is in **neither** model's pretraining corpus: a fair zero-shot test. Keep the size in view — the
  best pretrained model of 2025 beats the M3 winner of 2000, averaged with ETS, by about 3%.

## What a zero-shot forecast looks like {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: m3-examples
#| fig-align: center
examples = ["M1143", "M484", "M1176"]          # Chronos-Bolt's win, a tie, and a loss
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
for ax, uid in zip(axes, examples):
    hist = train_m3[train_m3["unique_id"] == uid].tail(48)
    fut = forecasts[forecasts["unique_id"] == uid]
    i = order.index(uid)
    ax.plot(hist["ds"], hist["y"], color=slate, linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["y"], color="black", linewidth=1, label="actual")
    ax.fill_between(fut["ds"], bolt_lo[i * H_M3:(i + 1) * H_M3], bolt_hi[i * H_M3:(i + 1) * H_M3],
                    color=red_pink, alpha=0.2, label="Chronos-Bolt 80%")
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["Chronos-Bolt"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="Chronos-Bolt")
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["ETS"], "--", color=blue, linewidth=1.5, label="ETS")
    mase_of = lambda c: np.mean(np.abs(fut["y"] - fut[c])) / scale_m3[uid]
    ax.set_title(f"{uid}: MASE  ETS {mase_of('ETS'):.2f},  Chronos-Bolt {mase_of('Chronos-Bolt'):.2f}", fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

- **M1143:** ETS extends the long upward trend; Chronos-Bolt reads the last two years' decline and
  follows it.
- **M484:** a noisy series with no clear pattern — both forecast a flat line, Chronos-Bolt with a wide,
  honest band.
- **M1176:** sharp yearly spikes. ETS reproduces them exactly; Chronos-Bolt flattens them, and loses
  five times over.

## Covariates: Chronos-2 and the 2026 World Cup {.smaller}

Messi's Wikipedia page views from Week 8, on logs. Chronos-2 was released in **October 2025**; the 2026
World Cup ran from 11 June to 19 July 2026. Whatever it forecasts here, it **cannot have seen**.

Stand on 10 June 2026 and forecast 51 days — once from the history alone, once with a **known future
covariate**: a 0/1 flag for tournament days, which anyone could write down from the fixture list.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
messi = pd.read_csv("../data/messi_wikipedia.csv", parse_dates=["ds"]).assign(item_id="messi")
messi["y"] = np.log(messi["y"])
tournaments = [("2016-06-03", 23), ("2018-06-14", 31), ("2019-06-14", 23), ("2021-06-13", 27),
               ("2022-11-20", 28), ("2024-06-20", 24), ("2026-06-11", 38)]
messi["tournament"] = 0
for start, days in tournaments:
    messi.loc[messi["ds"].between(start, pd.Timestamp(start) + pd.Timedelta(days=days)), "tournament"] = 1

H_WC = 51
history_wc = messi[messi["ds"] < "2026-06-11"]
future_wc = messi[messi["ds"] >= "2026-06-11"].head(H_WC)
settings = dict(id_column="item_id", timestamp_column="ds", target="y",
                prediction_length=H_WC, quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
alone = chronos2.predict_df(history_wc[["item_id", "ds", "y"]], **settings)
with_flag = chronos2.predict_df(history_wc[["item_id", "ds", "y", "tournament"]],
                                future_df=future_wc[["item_id", "ds", "tournament"]], **settings)
```

## The World Cup, forecast in advance {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: world-cup
#| fig-align: center
from prophet import Prophet
logging.getLogger("cmdstanpy").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
events = pd.DataFrame([{"holiday": "tournament", "ds": pd.Timestamp(s), "lower_window": 0, "upper_window": d}
                       for s, d in tournaments])
prophet_wc = Prophet(holidays=events).fit(history_wc[["ds", "y"]])
prophet_fc = prophet_wc.predict(future_wc[["ds"]])
actual_wc = future_wc["y"].to_numpy()
runs = {"Chronos-2, history only": (alone["predictions"], alone["0.1"], alone["0.9"], blue),
        "Chronos-2 + tournament flag": (with_flag["predictions"], with_flag["0.1"], with_flag["0.9"], red_pink),
        "Prophet + events table (Week 8)": (prophet_fc["yhat"], prophet_fc["yhat_lower"], prophet_fc["yhat_upper"], turquoise)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.6))
recent = messi[messi["ds"].between("2026-04-01", future_wc["ds"].max())]
ax.plot(recent["ds"], recent["y"], color=slate, linewidth=1.2, label="actual")
for name, (point, lo, hi, colour) in runs.items():
    ax.plot(future_wc["ds"], point, color=colour, linewidth=1.8, label=name)
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp("2026-06-11"), pd.Timestamp("2026-07-19"), color=orange, alpha=0.08)
ax.set_ylabel("log views")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("From 10 June 2026: 51 days ahead; the shaded weeks are the tournament")
plt.show()
```

The flag lifts the whole tournament period and brings the forecast down again after the final — the
shape is right. The **level** is not: every model stays far below the matches' peaks.

## What the flag bought {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
wc_scores = pd.DataFrame({
    name: {"MAE, log views": np.mean(np.abs(actual_wc - np.asarray(point))),
           "views forecast / actual": np.exp(np.asarray(point)).sum() / np.exp(actual_wc).sum(),
           "80% coverage": np.mean((actual_wc >= np.asarray(lo)) & (actual_wc <= np.asarray(hi)))}
    for name, (point, lo, hi, _) in runs.items()}).T
scoreboard(wc_scores, rules={"MAE, log views": "lower", "views forecast / actual": 1.0, "80% coverage": 0.80},
           decimals=2)
```

- **The flag helps.** The error falls from 1.31 to 0.87 log points and the interval's coverage from
  0.47 to 0.65. Chronos-2 reads the whole history (its context holds 8192 days) and takes what a
  tournament does to these views from the six earlier ones — **in-context learning**, with no
  parameter fitted to Messi.
- **Everyone under-forecasts.** The forecast totals are a fifth to a third of the views that actually
  came: this World Cup drew far more attention than the history implied.
- **Prophet with the same table does worst** — one "tournament" effect averaged over World Cups and the
  smaller Copas, and an interval with no error dynamics (Week 8) that covers 2% of the days.

## Did it see the answer? {.smaller}

A zero-shot score is only zero-shot if the test data were not in the pretraining corpus. For Chronos:

- **M4 Monthly** — all 48,000 series — is in the corpus of Chronos (the paper's "in-domain" benchmark)
  and of Chronos-2. The **last 18 months** of every series were held out of training.
- **M3 Monthly** is in neither corpus.

So on an M4 series the 18 months **before** the official test were seen in pretraining; the test itself
was not. If the model **remembers**, it should do unusually well on that earlier window.

| | window 1: months $-36$ to $-19$ | window 2: last 18 months |
|---|---|---|
| **M4** | seen in pretraining | held out |
| **M3** | never seen | never seen |

The test: Chronos's MASE **relative to ETS**, on 1000 series from each dataset, in each window. Memory
would show as a gain from window 2 to window 1 on M4 **larger than** the same gain on M3 — a
difference-in-differences. M3 absorbs everything about the two windows that has nothing to do with
memory.

## Seen and unseen windows {.smaller}

```{python}
#| code-summary: "The test, in code"
leak = pd.read_csv("../data/foundation_leakage.csv")   # built by infra/foundation_leakage.py


def memory_effect(df, model):
    """Geometric-mean MASE ratio to ETS: (M4 seen / M4 test) / (M3 / M3)."""
    r = np.log(df[model] / df["ETS"]).groupby([df["dataset"], df["window"]]).mean()
    return np.exp((r["M4", "pretraining window"] - r["M4", "held-out test"])
                  - (r["M3", "pretraining window"] - r["M3", "held-out test"]))


def resample(df, rng, n=None):
    """The same series in both windows: draw series, not rows."""
    parts = []
    for name, d in df.groupby("dataset"):
        ids = d["unique_id"].unique()
        pick = rng.choice(ids, n or len(ids), replace=n is None)
        parts.append(d.set_index("unique_id").loc[pick].reset_index())
    return pd.concat(parts)


rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rows = {}
for model in ["Chronos-Bolt", "Chronos-2", "snaive"]:
    boot = [memory_effect(resample(leak, rng), model) for _ in range(300)]
    rows[model] = {"memory effect": memory_effect(leak, model),
                   "2.5%": np.percentile(boot, 2.5), "97.5%": np.percentile(boot, 97.5)}
scoreboard(pd.DataFrame(rows).T, rules={"memory effect": 1.0})
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# How often does a 300-series sample show a "memory effect" below 0.95 when there is none?
pilots = np.array([memory_effect(resample(leak, np.random.default_rng(s), n=300), "Chronos-2")
                   for s in range(500)])
assert 0.08 < np.mean(pilots < 0.95) < 0.20, np.mean(pilots < 0.95)
```

- **No memory found.** Below 1 would mean Chronos does better on the window it saw; both sit at 1,
  intervals about 0.94–1.06. Chronos-2 beats ETS by about 6% in all four cells, seen or unseen.
- **The placebo shows the test can see.** Seasonal naive has no memory, yet its row moves (1.14,
  interval excluding 1): differences between the windows are detected when they exist.
- **Small tests mislead.** A first run on 300 series per dataset gave 0.94 — "6% memory". With no
  effect at all, about one 300-series sample in seven shows that much.

Not shown: that the corpus is harmless. If your holdout itself were in it, only the release date
would protect you.

## A zero-shot comparison you can trust {.smaller}

The final project asks for one (2 points, for the setup — not for who wins). The checklist:

1. **Same cutoff, same horizon, same metric** as your own model. The foundation model gets the
   training history as its context and nothing after it.
2. **No tuning on the holdout.** Choosing among five foundation models by their test score is
   selection on the test set — Week 3's oldest mistake.
3. **Check the corpus.** Find the model's list of training datasets (Chronos: the paper's Table 3;
   Chronos-2: Table 6). If your data, or a famous public version of it, is on the list, say so.
4. **Check the dates.** A model released before your holdout period began cannot have seen the holdout.
   That is the one guarantee that does not depend on anyone's documentation.
5. **Report the interval too.** A zero-shot model's quantiles are a forecast like any other: score
   their coverage, as in Week 8.

# Wrapping up

## Eight ways to get this wrong {.tiny}

| Trap | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A neural network on 100 observations | A perfect fit, a wild forecast | Few weights, or a global model, or a simpler model |
| One random seed | A different forecast every run | Average several networks, or fix and report the seed |
| Unscaled inputs to a network | Training that never converges | Scale each series first |
| A global model on incomparable series | Big series dominate the loss | Scale per series: `LocalStandardScaler`, `scaler_type` |
| Neural results without a benchmark | "LSTM: MAE 412" — and nothing to compare it with | Seasonal naive and ETS on the same holdout, always |
| Zero-shot scored on data in the pretraining corpus | Results that look too good | Check the corpus list and the release date |
| Picking the foundation model by test score | An optimistic comparison | Choose on validation windows, report on the test |
| "Pretrained" read as "better" | A slower, opaque model that loses to Theta | It is one more candidate on the rolling origin |

## What this lecture is, in one slide {.smaller}

- **NNAR** is an autoregression with a hidden layer: non-linear, local, averaged over random starts,
  with intervals by simulation. It needs long series.
- **Global models** pool many series after scaling each: LightGBM on lags, N-HiTS, LSTM. They borrow
  strength across series; that is what makes deep learning work on short series at all.
- **Recurrent networks** carry a state forward; the **LSTM** keeps it with gates — ETS's "keep most of
  the old, add a little of the new", learned.
- **Foundation models** are global models trained on everything available, applied **zero-shot**.
  They are fast, easy, often strong — and their test is only honest if the test data were not in the
  corpus.
